2 Chronicles.line: The history of Judah from Solomon to the exile, showing God's faithfulness to David's line and the temple.
more: Solomon receives wisdom, builds the temple in Jerusalem, and God fills it with his glory.
After Solomon, the northern tribes break away, and the account follows Judah's kings.
Each king is judged by whether he seeks the LORD and keeps his covenant.
Reforms under Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah bring renewal, while unfaithful kings bring judgment.
Persistent rebellion leads Babylon to destroy Jerusalem and the temple and take the people into exile.
The book closes with Cyrus decreeing that the exiles may return and rebuild the temple.

1.line: At Gibeon, Solomon asks God for wisdom to govern, and God grants wisdom along with great wealth.
more: Solomon worships with the assembly at the bronze altar before the tabernacle at Gibeon.
God appears at night and invites Solomon to ask for whatever he wishes.
Solomon's chariots, horses, silver, and gold multiply, and he trades with Egypt.

2.line: Solomon prepares to build the temple and secures materials and a skilled craftsman from Hiram king of Tyre.
more: Solomon explains that the temple is for incense and offerings to the great God.
Hiram praises the LORD and sends Huram-abi, skilled in metal, stone, wood, and fabrics.
Solomon conscripts the foreigners living in Israel as laborers, stonecutters, and overseers.

3.line: Solomon begins building the temple on Mount Moriah, overlaying it with gold and adorning the Most Holy Place.
more: The site is Ornan's threshing floor, where the LORD had appeared to David.
Two large golden cherubim stand in the Most Holy Place, which is screened by a woven veil.
Two bronze pillars named Jachin and Boaz stand before the temple.

4.line: The temple's furnishings are made, including the bronze altar, the great bronze sea, basins, lampstands, and tables.
more: The cast sea rests on twelve bronze oxen and is used by the priests for washing.
Huram completes the bronze work, cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain.
Solomon makes the golden altar, lampstands, and other gold vessels for the inner house.

5.line: The ark is brought into the temple, and as the singers praise God, a cloud of glory fills the house.
more: Solomon places the treasures David had dedicated in the temple storehouses.
The priests set the ark beneath the cherubim; it holds only the two tablets.
The priests cannot stand to minister because of the cloud.

6.line: Solomon blesses the assembly and prays at the temple's dedication, asking God to hear prayers offered toward this house.
more: Solomon recounts God's promise to David that his son would build the temple.
He acknowledges that heaven cannot contain God, much less this house.
He asks God to forgive and restore in times of sin, defeat, drought, plague, and exile.
He also asks God to hear foreigners who pray toward the temple.

7.line: Fire falls from heaven on the sacrifices, and God answers Solomon with promises and warnings.
more: The people bow in worship, and Solomon offers vast sacrifices during a festival of dedication.
God promises to forgive and heal the land if his humbled people pray and turn.
He warns that turning to other gods will bring uprooting and the temple's ruin.

8.line: Solomon builds cities, organizes forced labor and temple worship, and sends ships to Ophir for gold.
more: He rebuilds cities given by Hiram and fortifies store cities and chariot cities.
He moves Pharaoh's daughter out of David's city because of the ark's holiness.
He arranges offerings and priestly and Levitical duties according to David's instructions.

9.line: The queen of Sheba visits and praises Solomon's wisdom; his wealth is described, and after forty years he dies.
more: The queen tests Solomon with hard questions and blesses the LORD who made him king.
Solomon's gold, ivory throne, and trade surpass all the kings of the earth.
Solomon is buried in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam reigns.

10.line: Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice and answers the people harshly, so the northern tribes rebel under Jeroboam.
more: Jeroboam returns from Egypt, and the people ask Rehoboam to lighten Solomon's heavy yoke.
Rehoboam follows his young companions and promises an even heavier yoke.
The text says God brought about this turn of affairs to fulfill his word.

11.line: God forbids Rehoboam to fight Israel, so he fortifies Judah, and priests and Levites from the north join him.
more: The prophet Shemaiah delivers God's command, and Rehoboam obeys.
Jeroboam rejects the Levites, so they and faithful Israelites move to Jerusalem, strengthening Judah for three years.
Rehoboam has many wives and children and appoints Abijah as chief prince.

12.line: When Rehoboam abandons God's law, Shishak of Egypt invades, but repentance spares Judah from complete destruction.
more: Shemaiah announces that because they abandoned God, God has abandoned them to Shishak.
The leaders humble themselves, and God grants some deliverance while making them Shishak's servants.
Shishak takes the temple and palace treasures; Rehoboam did evil and dies after seventeen years.

13.line: Abijah of Judah challenges Jeroboam, and though outnumbered and ambushed, Judah wins because they rely on the LORD.
more: Abijah declares that God gave David's line the kingdom and that Judah keeps the true priesthood.
Judah cries to the LORD, the priests blow trumpets, and God defeats Israel.
Jeroboam never recovers his power and dies, while Abijah grows strong.

14.line: Asa does what is right, removes idols, and defeats a vast Ethiopian army under Zerah by relying on God.
more: Asa commands Judah to seek the LORD and keep his law, and the land has rest.
He fortifies cities and builds an army during the years of peace.
Asa prays for help, and God strikes the Ethiopians, who flee before Judah.

15.line: Encouraged by the prophet Azariah, Asa removes idols and leads Judah in a covenant to seek the LORD.
more: Azariah says the LORD is with them while they seek him, and he will be found.
Many from the north join Asa, and the people swear the covenant with joy.
Asa removes his grandmother Maacah as queen mother for her idol, though high places remain.

16.line: Late in his reign Asa relies on Syria rather than God, imprisons the prophet who rebukes him, and dies diseased.
more: Asa pays Ben-hadad with temple treasures to break his treaty with Baasha of Israel.
Hanani the seer rebukes him for relying on Syria instead of the LORD.
Asa angrily jails Hanani, and in his foot disease he seeks physicians rather than the LORD.

17.line: Jehoshaphat seeks God, strengthens Judah, and sends officials and Levites to teach the Book of the Law.
more: He walks in David's early ways and removes high places and Asherah poles.
The fear of the LORD falls on surrounding kingdoms, and some bring him tribute.
He builds fortresses and store cities and commands a large army.

18.line: Jehoshaphat allies with Ahab against Ramoth-gilead, ignoring Micaiah's warning, and Ahab is killed in battle.
more: Jehoshaphat makes a marriage alliance with Ahab and agrees to go to war.
Ahab's prophets promise victory, but Micaiah foresees Israel scattered and describes a lying spirit.
Jehoshaphat cries out and is spared, while a random arrow fatally wounds the disguised Ahab.

19.line: Rebuked for helping Ahab, Jehoshaphat brings the people back to the LORD and appoints judges throughout Judah.
more: Jehu the seer says wrath is on him, yet some good is found in him.
Jehoshaphat charges judges to judge in the fear of the LORD, without partiality or bribes.
He sets priests and Levites in Jerusalem to decide disputes, under Amariah and Zebadiah.

20.line: Facing a vast invading army, Jehoshaphat leads Judah in prayer, and God makes the enemies destroy one another.
more: Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast and prays, confessing they do not know what to do.
Jahaziel declares the battle is God's, and singers lead the army out in praise.
Judah gathers plunder for three days and blesses God in the Valley of Beracah.
Jehoshaphat's shipping alliance with Ahaziah of Israel ends in wrecked ships, as a prophet foretold.

21.line: Jehoram kills his brothers and follows Ahab's ways, suffering revolt, invasion, and a painful death without mourning.
more: Married to Ahab's daughter, he does evil, yet God spares David's line because of his covenant.
Edom and Libnah revolt, and a letter from Elijah announces judgment on Jehoram.
Philistines and Arabians carry off his possessions and sons, and he dies of a bowel disease.

22.line: Ahaziah reigns briefly and is killed by Jehu, then Athaliah seizes power and murders the royal family except Joash.
more: Ahaziah follows the counsel of his mother Athaliah and Ahab's house, doing evil.
Visiting Joram of Israel, he is caught up in Jehu's judgment on Ahab's house.
Jehoshabeath hides the infant Joash in the temple for six years.

23.line: The priest Jehoiada crowns young Joash king, Athaliah is executed, and the people renew their covenant with the LORD.
more: Jehoiada organizes Levites and commanders to guard the king inside the temple.
Athaliah cries treason and is put to death outside the temple.
The people tear down Baal's house, and worship is restored as David ordered.

24.line: Joash repairs the temple while Jehoiada lives, but afterward turns to idols, has Zechariah stoned, and is assassinated.
more: A chest collects the tax Moses commanded, funding the temple repairs.
Jehoiada dies honored, and the officials lead Joash and Judah into idolatry.
Jehoiada's son Zechariah warns them and is stoned in the temple court at the king's command.
A small Syrian army defeats Judah, and Joash's servants kill him in his bed.

25.line: Amaziah defeats Edom but then worships Edom's gods, and he is defeated by Israel and later assassinated.
more: He does right, but not with a whole heart.
At a prophet's warning, he sends home hired Israelite soldiers, who then raid Judah's towns.
He rejects a prophet's rebuke and provokes Joash of Israel, who breaks down Jerusalem's wall.

26.line: Uzziah prospers greatly while seeking God, but in pride he burns incense in the temple and is struck with leprosy.
more: He seeks God in the days of Zechariah, who instructs him in the fear of God.
He defeats enemies, builds towers, loves farming, and develops a strong, well-equipped army.
Azariah and the priests confront him, and he lives isolated with leprosy until his death.

27.line: Jotham does what is right, builds and fortifies, subdues the Ammonites, and becomes mighty because he walks before God.
more: Unlike his father, he does not enter the temple, but the people still act corruptly.
He builds the upper gate of the temple and fortified cities and towers.
He reigns sixteen years and is succeeded by his son Ahaz.

28.line: Ahaz practices idolatry, suffers heavy defeats, seeks help from Assyria, and finally shuts the doors of the temple.
more: He burns his sons as offerings and worships at high places.
Syria and Israel defeat Judah, but the prophet Oded persuades Israel to return the captives.
Edomites and Philistines also attack, and Assyria's king afflicts rather than helps him.
Ahaz sacrifices to Syria's gods and sets up altars throughout Jerusalem.

29.line: Hezekiah reopens the temple, has the priests and Levites cleanse it, and restores sacrifice and worship.
more: In his first month he calls the Levites to consecrate themselves and remove the filth.
Sin offerings are made to atone for all Israel, with music as David commanded.
The assembly brings so many offerings that Levites help the priests, and all rejoice.

30.line: Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah to a great Passover in Jerusalem, celebrated with joy unknown since Solomon.
more: Couriers carry letters into the north; many mock, but some humble themselves and come.
The feast is held in the second month because priests had not consecrated themselves in time.
Hezekiah prays for those eating while unclean, and God heals the people.
The assembly extends the festival seven more days.

31.line: The people destroy idols throughout the land, and Hezekiah organizes priests and Levites and their support from tithes.
more: The people bring tithes and offerings in heaps over several months.
Storerooms are prepared, and officials distribute portions fairly to priests, Levites, and their families.
Hezekiah does what is good and seeks God with all his heart, and he prospers.

32.line: Sennacherib of Assyria invades and mocks God, but after Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, an angel destroys the Assyrian army.
more: Hezekiah blocks springs, strengthens walls, and encourages the people that God is with them.
Sennacherib returns home in shame and is killed by his own sons.
Hezekiah recovers from illness but becomes proud, then humbles himself; God tests him through Babylon's envoys.
Hezekiah channels the Gihon waters into the city, prospers, and dies honored.

33.line: Manasseh leads Judah into deep evil, is taken captive to Babylon, repents, and is restored; his son Amon is assassinated.
more: Manasseh rebuilds high places, worships the stars, burns his sons, and practices sorcery.
In distress he humbles himself and prays, and God brings him back to Jerusalem.
He removes foreign gods and restores the altar, though people still use high places.
Amon does evil without humbling himself, and his servants kill him after two years.

34.line: Josiah purges idolatry, repairs the temple, and after the Book of the Law is found, leads Judah in covenant renewal.
more: He begins seeking God as a youth and destroys idols in Judah and the north.
Hearing the law read, Josiah tears his clothes, and the prophetess Huldah is consulted.
Huldah announces coming disaster but says Josiah will die in peace because he humbled himself.
Josiah and the people pledge to keep the covenant, and they do so all his days.

35.line: Josiah keeps an unmatched Passover, then dies after ignoring Pharaoh Neco's warning and fighting him at Megiddo.
more: The ark is placed in the temple, and priests and Levites serve in their divisions.
No Passover like it had been kept since the days of Samuel.
The text says Neco's words came from God, but Josiah disguised himself and fought.
All Judah mourns Josiah, and Jeremiah composes a lament for him.

36.line: Judah's last kings do evil, Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple, and decades later Cyrus permits the return.
more: Jehoahaz is deposed by Egypt, and Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin are taken to Babylon.
Zedekiah rebels and refuses Jeremiah's word, while leaders and people defile the temple.
God repeatedly sent messengers, but they mocked them until there was no remedy.
The land keeps its Sabbaths for seventy years, fulfilling Jeremiah's word.

Ezra.line: Jews return from exile in Persia, rebuild the temple, and are reformed under Ezra's teaching of God's law.
more: Cyrus decrees that the exiles may return, and a first group goes back to Jerusalem.
They rebuild the altar and lay the temple foundation, but opponents halt the work.
Encouraged by Haggai and Zechariah, they finish the temple under Darius and celebrate Passover.
Decades later Ezra the scribe leads another group to Jerusalem to teach the law.
Ezra confronts intermarriage with surrounding peoples, and the people confess and put away foreign wives.

1.line: Cyrus king of Persia decrees that the Jews may return to Jerusalem to rebuild the LORD's house.
more: The text says God stirred Cyrus's spirit, fulfilling Jeremiah's word.
Family heads, priests, and Levites prepare to go, and neighbors give them supplies and gifts.
Cyrus returns the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar took, entrusting them to Sheshbazzar.

2.line: A list records the exiles who returned with Zerubbabel, by family, town, and temple service.
more: The list includes priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and descendants of Solomon's servants.
Priests unable to prove their genealogy are excluded from the priesthood until a ruling.
The whole assembly numbers 42,360, and family heads give freewill offerings for the temple.

3.line: The returned exiles rebuild the altar, resume sacrifices, and lay the temple foundation amid shouts and weeping.
more: Jeshua and Zerubbabel build the altar despite fear of the surrounding peoples.
They keep the Feast of Booths and order cedar from Lebanon.
Older people who had seen the first temple weep while others shout for joy.

4.line: Local opponents offer to help, are refused, and then frustrate the rebuilding until the work stops.
more: Adversaries discourage the builders and hire counselors against them through the reign of Cyrus.
A later letter to Artaxerxes accuses Jerusalem of rebellion, and he orders the city's building stopped.
Work on the temple ceases until the second year of Darius.

5.line: Prompted by Haggai and Zechariah, the Jews resume building, and the governor Tattenai writes to Darius about it.
more: Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin rebuilding with the prophets supporting them.
God's eye is on the elders, so the work is not stopped during the inquiry.
The elders explain that Cyrus had authorized the temple's rebuilding.

6.line: Darius finds Cyrus's decree and orders support for the temple, which is completed, dedicated, and followed by Passover.
more: Darius commands Tattenai to fund the work and supply sacrifices, threatening anyone who interferes.
The temple is finished in Darius's sixth year and dedicated with joy.
The returned exiles and those who separated from impurity keep Passover and Unleavened Bread.

7.line: Ezra, a priest and scribe skilled in the law, travels to Jerusalem with authority from King Artaxerxes.
more: Ezra had set his heart to study, do, and teach the LORD's law.
Artaxerxes's letter provides funds, temple offerings, tax exemptions, and authority to appoint judges.
Ezra blesses God for putting this in the king's heart.

8.line: Ezra gathers returnees and Levites, fasts for protection rather than requesting soldiers, and arrives safely with the treasures.
more: The family heads who return with Ezra are listed.
Finding no Levites, Ezra recruits Levites and temple servants from Casiphia.
Priests guard the weighed silver, gold, and vessels, which are handed over in Jerusalem.

9.line: Learning that many have intermarried with surrounding peoples, Ezra mourns and confesses Israel's guilt to God in prayer.
more: Officials report that people, priests, and Levites took wives from peoples practicing abominations.
Ezra tears his garments and sits appalled until the evening sacrifice.
He acknowledges that God punished them less than deserved and left them a remnant.

10.line: The people agree to put away their foreign wives, an inquiry is held, and the offenders are listed.
more: Shecaniah proposes a covenant, and Ezra makes the leaders swear to act.
The assembly gathers in heavy rain and asks that officials handle the cases over time.
The final list names priests, Levites, and others who had married foreign women.

Nehemiah.line: Nehemiah returns from Persia to rebuild Jerusalem's walls and, with Ezra, restores the people to covenant faithfulness.
more: Grieved by Jerusalem's ruin, Nehemiah prays and receives the king's permission to rebuild.
Despite mockery, threats, and schemes, the people complete the wall in fifty-two days.
Ezra reads the law, and the people confess their sins and seal a covenant.
Jerusalem is repopulated, and the walls are dedicated with joyful worship.
Returning later, Nehemiah confronts renewed failures regarding the temple, the Sabbath, and intermarriage.

1.line: Hearing that Jerusalem's walls are broken down, Nehemiah weeps, fasts, and prays to God for favor with the king.
more: Nehemiah serves as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes in Susa.
He confesses Israel's sins and recalls God's promise to gather a repentant people.
He asks for success when he approaches the king.

2.line: Artaxerxes grants Nehemiah's request to rebuild Jerusalem, and Nehemiah inspects the walls by night and rallies the people.
more: The king notices his sadness, and Nehemiah prays before asking for leave, letters, and timber.
Sanballat and Tobiah are displeased that someone seeks Israel's welfare.
When opponents mock, Nehemiah answers that God will make them prosper.

3.line: A list records who rebuilt each section of the wall and gates, working side by side.
more: Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests begin with the Sheep Gate.
Families, goldsmiths, perfumers, merchants, and district rulers repair sections, often near their own houses.
The nobles of Tekoa refuse to do the work.

4.line: Opponents mock and plot to attack, so Nehemiah prays, posts guards, and has the builders work armed.
more: Sanballat and Tobiah ridicule the work, and Nehemiah asks God to judge them.
The wall reaches half its height because the people have a mind to work.
Half the men stand guard while the others build with weapons at hand.

5.line: Nehemiah confronts nobles who exploit poor Jews through interest and debt slavery, and they agree to restore what they took.
more: Families complain of hunger, mortgaged fields, and children sold into slavery.
Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, who promise to return fields and stop charging interest.
As governor, he declines the governor's food allowance and feeds many at his own expense.

6.line: Nehemiah resists his enemies' schemes, and the wall is finished in fifty-two days.
more: Sanballat repeatedly invites Nehemiah to meet, intending harm, and sends a letter alleging rebellion.
Shemaiah, a hired prophet, urges him to hide in the temple, but Nehemiah refuses.
Surrounding nations lose confidence, perceiving the work was done with God's help.

7.line: Nehemiah appoints guards for Jerusalem and finds the genealogy of the first returnees, preparing to repopulate the city.
more: He puts Hanani and Hananiah in charge, ordering the gates kept shut until the sun is hot.
The city is large, but it has few people and few houses.
The list of returnees from Zerubbabel's time is repeated, along with gifts for the work.

8.line: Ezra reads the law to the assembled people, who weep, then rejoice and keep the Feast of Booths.
more: Levites help the people understand the reading.
Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites say the day is holy and the joy of the LORD is their strength.
The people make booths and celebrate for seven days, as not done since Joshua.

9.line: The people fast and confess their sins, and the Levites pray a long review of God's faithfulness and Israel's rebellion.
more: The prayer recounts creation, Abraham, the exodus, Sinai, the wilderness, and the conquest.
It recalls repeated rebellion in the land and God's merciful deliverances.
They acknowledge they are slaves under foreign kings and make a firm written covenant.

10.line: Leaders, priests, and Levites seal a covenant, and the people pledge to keep God's law.
more: Nehemiah heads the list of those who set their seals.
They promise not to intermarry with surrounding peoples or trade on the Sabbath.
They pledge the temple tax, wood, firstfruits, and tithes, vowing not to neglect God's house.

11.line: One in ten is chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem, and those who settle there and in Judah are listed.
more: The people bless those who willingly offer to live in Jerusalem.
Leaders of Judah and Benjamin, priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in Jerusalem are named.
The towns and villages where others settle are also listed.

12.line: Priests and Levites are listed, and the wall is dedicated with two great choirs and joyful sacrifices.
more: The list covers priests and Levites from Zerubbabel's return through later generations.
Two thanksgiving choirs walk the wall in opposite directions and meet at the temple.
The joy of Jerusalem is heard far away, and men are appointed over the storerooms.

13.line: Returning after an absence, Nehemiah corrects abuses involving Tobiah, temple support, the Sabbath, and intermarriage.
more: He throws Tobiah's belongings out of a temple storeroom that Eliashib the priest had given him.
He restores the Levites' portions and stops Sabbath trading by shutting the gates.
He rebukes Jews who married foreign women, recalling Solomon's sin.
He repeatedly asks God to remember him for good.

Esther.line: Esther, a Jewish queen of Persia, and her cousin Mordecai thwart Haman's plot to destroy the Jews.
more: King Ahasuerus deposes Queen Vashti and chooses Esther, whose Jewish identity stays hidden.
Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, who secures a decree to annihilate all Jews.
Esther risks her life to approach the king and exposes Haman at a banquet.
Haman is hanged, Mordecai is promoted, and the Jews are permitted to defend themselves.
The Jews prevail over their enemies, and the Feast of Purim is established to remember it.
God is never named, yet events repeatedly turn in favor of his people.

1.line: King Ahasuerus holds lavish feasts, and when Queen Vashti refuses his summons, she is removed as queen.
more: The king displays his wealth for 180 days, then holds a seven-day feast in Susa.
His advisers warn that Vashti's refusal will encourage wives to despise their husbands.
A decree bars Vashti from the king's presence and declares men masters of their households.

2.line: Esther is chosen queen from among the young women gathered, and Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.
more: Mordecai, a Benjaminite exile, raised his orphaned cousin Hadassah, also called Esther.
Esther wins favor and, at Mordecai's instruction, does not reveal her people.
Mordecai reports two eunuchs' assassination plot through Esther, and it is recorded in the chronicles.

3.line: When Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, Haman obtains a royal decree to destroy all the Jews.
more: Haman the Agagite is promoted above all the king's officials.
Lots, called Pur, are cast to choose the date, falling in the twelfth month.
Haman offers silver to the treasury, the decree goes out, and Susa is thrown into confusion.

4.line: Mordecai mourns and urges Esther to plead with the king, and she resolves to go despite the risk of death.
more: Jews throughout the provinces fast, weep, and lament.
Esther explains that approaching the king unsummoned means death unless he extends his scepter.
Mordecai says she may have come to royal position for such a time; Esther asks all Jews to fast.

5.line: The king receives Esther, who invites him and Haman to banquets, while Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai.
more: At the first banquet Esther delays her request and invites them back the next day.
Haman leaves joyful but is enraged when Mordecai again refuses to rise or tremble.
His wife Zeresh and his friends advise a gallows fifty cubits high.

6.line: On a sleepless night the king learns Mordecai was never rewarded, and Haman is forced to honor him publicly.
more: The chronicles read to the king record how Mordecai exposed the assassination plot.
Haman, assuming the king means him, proposes royal robes and a horse led through the city.
Haman's wife and advisers predict his downfall before Mordecai, and he is hurried to the banquet.

7.line: At the second banquet Esther reveals her identity and Haman's plot, and Haman is hanged on his own gallows.
more: Esther asks for her life and her people's lives, since they have been sold for destruction.
The furious king steps out, and Haman falls on Esther's couch pleading for his life.
Harbona mentions the gallows, and the king orders Haman hanged on it.

8.line: Mordecai is promoted, and a new decree allows the Jews to defend themselves against anyone who attacks them.
more: The king gives Haman's house to Esther and his signet ring to Mordecai.
Esther pleads to revoke Haman's plot, but a royal decree cannot be revoked.
Couriers carry the new edict, and many from other peoples declare themselves Jews.

9.line: On the appointed day the Jews defeat their enemies, and Purim is established as an annual feast of celebration.
more: Officials help the Jews out of fear of Mordecai, and Haman's ten sons are killed.
At Esther's request, the Jews of Susa defend themselves a second day, but they take no plunder.
Mordecai and Esther write letters confirming the days of Purim for all generations.

10.line: The book closes noting King Ahasuerus's power and Mordecai's greatness as second only to the king.
more: Mordecai's acts are recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia.
He is popular among the Jews, seeking their welfare and speaking peace to them.

Job.line: Job, a righteous man, suffers terrible loss, wrestles with God's justice alongside his friends, and finally meets God himself.
more: In heaven Satan challenges Job's devotion, and God permits him to take Job's wealth, children, and health.
Three friends come to comfort Job and argue that his suffering must be punishment for sin.
Job insists on his innocence, laments his condition, and longs to plead his case before God.
Elihu, a younger man, rebukes both Job and the friends, emphasizing God's greatness and discipline.
God speaks from the whirlwind, displaying his power and wisdom in creation, and Job repents.
God rebukes the friends, accepts Job's prayer for them, and restores Job's fortunes twofold.

1.line: Satan challenges the righteous Job's devotion, and God permits him to strike all Job's possessions and children.
more: Job of Uz is blameless, very wealthy, and regularly offers sacrifices for his children.
Satan claims Job fears God only because God protects and blesses him.
Raiders and disasters destroy Job's flocks, servants, and children in one day.
Job tears his robe and worships, and he does not sin or charge God with wrong.

2.line: Satan afflicts Job with painful sores, yet Job still does not sin, and three friends come to comfort him.
more: God permits Satan to strike Job's body but spare his life.
Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, but he rebukes her.
Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar sit silently with Job for seven days.

3.line: Job breaks his silence and curses the day of his birth, wishing he had never lived.
more: He longs for the rest of the grave, where the weary find peace.
He asks why life is given to those in misery.
He says what he feared has come upon him, and he has no rest.

4.line: Eliphaz answers that the innocent do not perish, implying Job's suffering must result from wrongdoing.
more: He reminds Job that he once strengthened others but now is dismayed.
He says those who plow iniquity reap trouble.
He describes a night vision asking whether mortals can be right before God.

5.line: Eliphaz urges Job to seek God and accept his discipline, promising restoration if he does.
more: He says trouble does not sprout from the ground, yet man is born to trouble.
He praises God's wondrous works and his rescue of the lowly.
He calls blessed the one God reproves and promises safety and prosperity.

6.line: Job replies that his anguish is heavier than sand and that his friends have failed him like dry streams.
more: He feels God's arrows within him and wishes God would crush him.
He asks his friends to show him where he has gone wrong.
He insists his integrity is still at stake.

7.line: Job laments life's misery and brevity and asks God why he will not leave him alone.
more: He compares life to hard service and his days to a weaver's shuttle.
He says God terrifies him with dreams and visions.
He asks why God does not pardon his sin before he dies.

8.line: Bildad argues that God does not pervert justice, suggesting Job's children died for their sin.
more: He urges Job to seek God, who will restore him if he is pure.
He appeals to the wisdom of earlier generations.
He compares the godless to plants that wither without water.

9.line: Job agrees God is just but asks how anyone can be right before so powerful a God.
more: He describes God moving mountains, shaking the earth, and making the stars.
He fears God would crush him and condemn him despite his innocence.
He wishes for an arbiter who could lay a hand on both of them.

10.line: Job speaks to God in bitterness, asking why the Creator who formed him now seeks to destroy him.
more: He asks God not to condemn him but to show why he contends with him.
He recalls being fashioned and cared for by God.
He wishes he had died at birth and asks for a little comfort before death.

11.line: Zophar rebukes Job's claims of innocence and says God exacts less than his guilt deserves.
more: He says God's wisdom is deeper than Sheol and beyond searching out.
He urges Job to put away iniquity and stretch out his hands to God.
He promises security and hope if Job repents, while the wicked lose hope.

12.line: Job sarcastically answers his friends and asserts that God's sovereign power governs all creation and human affairs.
more: He says he has become a laughingstock though he called on God.
The beasts and birds know that God's hand has done this.
God overturns counselors, judges, kings, and nations at his will.

13.line: Job calls his friends worthless physicians and resolves to argue his case directly before God.
more: He warns that their false words on God's behalf will not escape God's rebuke.
He resolves to hope in God even if God slays him, believing he will be vindicated.
He asks God to withdraw his hand and make known his sins.

14.line: Job reflects on the brevity of human life and wonders whether a person who dies can live again.
more: He says a tree may sprout again, but mortals lie down and do not rise.
He longs for God to hide him in Sheol until his wrath passes.
He feels God destroys human hope as water wears away stones.

15.line: Eliphaz condemns Job's words as undermining the fear of God and describes the torment of the wicked.
more: He says Job's own mouth condemns him.
He asks whether Job thinks he alone has wisdom.
He describes the wicked living in terror and losing their wealth.

16.line: Job calls his friends miserable comforters and describes God's assault on him, yet appeals to a witness in heaven.
more: He says he could speak as they do if their places were reversed.
He describes God tearing him and handing him over to the ungodly.
He insists his prayer is pure and hopes his witness will plead for him.

17.line: Job says his spirit is broken and his days are ending, and he finds no wise person among his friends.
more: He asks God to give a pledge for him, since no one else will.
He has become a byword, and his eyes have grown dim.
He sees only Sheol ahead and asks where his hope is.

18.line: Bildad describes in vivid images how the wicked are trapped, terrified, and forgotten.
more: He resents Job treating the friends as stupid.
He says the light of the wicked is put out.
He says such is the dwelling of one who does not know God.

19.line: Job protests that God has wronged him and everyone has abandoned him, yet declares that his Redeemer lives.
more: He says God has walled up his way and counts him an enemy.
Relatives, friends, servants, and even his wife have turned from him.
He is confident that in his flesh he will see God.
He warns his friends to fear judgment for pursuing him.

20.line: Zophar says the triumph of the wicked is brief and their gains are taken away by God's anger.
more: He feels insulted by Job's rebuke and answers from his understanding.
He says the wicked must give back the riches they swallowed.
He calls this the heritage God appoints for the wicked.

21.line: Job argues against his friends that the wicked often prosper, live long, and die in peace.
more: Their children flourish, their livestock thrive, and they tell God to depart.
He questions how often their lamp is actually put out.
He says the friends' comfort is empty and their answers false.

22.line: Eliphaz accuses Job of specific sins, such as mistreating the poor, and urges him to return to God.
more: He says God does not reprove Job for his piety.
He alleges Job stripped the naked and withheld water and bread from the needy.
He promises restoration and delight in God if Job agrees with God and returns.

23.line: Job longs to find God and present his case, confident God would hear, yet he cannot find him.
more: He looks forward, backward, left, and right but does not perceive God.
He says God knows his way and that he will come out as gold.
He has kept God's words, yet he is terrified of God.

24.line: Job describes the oppression of the poor and the crimes of the wicked, asking why God does not set times of judgment.
more: The poor go hungry and naked while the wicked move boundaries and seize flocks.
Murderers, adulterers, and thieves prefer darkness.
He acknowledges the wicked eventually perish and challenges anyone to prove him wrong.

25.line: Bildad briefly declares God's dominion and asks how any mortal can be righteous before him.
more: He notes that even the moon and stars are not pure in God's sight.
He calls man a maggot and a worm by comparison.

26.line: Job mocks Bildad's help and describes God's vast power over the deep, the heavens, and the sea.
more: Sheol is naked before God, and he hangs the earth on nothing.
God stills the sea and pierces the fleeing serpent.
Job says these are but the outskirts of God's ways.

27.line: Job vows to maintain his integrity and describes the eventual fate of the wicked.
more: He swears he will not speak falsehood or deny his innocence while he lives.
He says the godless have no hope when God takes their life.
The children, wealth, and house of the wicked will not last.

28.line: A poem asks where wisdom can be found and concludes that only God knows its way.
more: Miners search the depths for silver, gold, and gems, but wisdom is not found there.
Wisdom cannot be bought with gold or precious stones.
God says the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and turning from evil is understanding.

29.line: Job recalls his former days when God watched over him and he was honored for helping the needy.
more: His children were around him, and he enjoyed abundance.
Young and old respected him at the city gate.
He rescued the poor, the fatherless, and the widow, and expected to die in his nest.

30.line: Job laments that he is now mocked by the lowest of men and that God has cast him into the mire.
more: Young men whose fathers he disdained now spit at him.
He cries to God but feels God does not answer and has turned cruel.
His skin turns black, and his music becomes mourning.

31.line: Job swears a series of oaths affirming his innocence and calls on God to answer him.
more: He denies lust, deceit, adultery, and mistreating his servants.
He denies neglecting the poor, trusting in gold, worshiping the sun or moon, or gloating over enemies.
He signs his defense and asks the Almighty to answer, and his words end.

32.line: Young Elihu, angry at Job and the three friends, begins to speak after waiting for his elders.
more: He is angry that Job justified himself rather than God.
He is angry that the friends condemned Job yet found no answer.
He says it is the spirit in man that gives understanding, not age alone.

33.line: Elihu tells Job that God speaks in many ways, through dreams and suffering, to turn people from pride and death.
more: He invites Job to answer him as an equal formed from clay.
He rejects Job's claim that God finds occasions against him.
He describes a mediator who may intercede, leading to restoration and confession.

34.line: Elihu insists God cannot do wickedness or pervert justice and charges Job with speaking without knowledge.
more: He objects to Job saying it profits nothing to delight in God.
God repays people according to their work and sees all their ways.
He says Job adds rebellion to his sin.

35.line: Elihu argues that human righteousness or sin does not affect God, and that God does not answer empty cries.
more: He tells Job to look at the heavens, which are higher than he.
People cry out under oppression but do not seek God their Maker.
He says Job multiplies words without knowledge.

36.line: Elihu says God uses affliction to instruct, then begins praising God's greatness displayed in the storm.
more: God does not despise anyone, and he opens ears by adversity.
He warns Job not to choose iniquity rather than affliction.
God is exalted in power, and his years are unsearchable.

37.line: Elihu concludes by describing God's majesty in thunder, snow, and storm, beyond human understanding.
more: God's voice thunders, and he commands snow and rain.
He asks whether Job can spread out the skies like God.
The Almighty is great in power and justice and does not regard the self-wise.

38.line: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, questioning him about the foundations and workings of creation.
more: He asks who darkens counsel by words without knowledge.
He asks where Job was when he laid the earth's foundation.
He questions Job about the sea, dawn, death, light, weather, stars, and feeding animals.

39.line: God continues questioning Job about wild animals whose lives and instincts are beyond human control.
more: He asks about mountain goats, the wild donkey, and the wild ox.
He describes the ostrich's lack of wisdom and the warhorse's fearlessness.
He asks whether the hawk and eagle soar by Job's wisdom.

40.line: Job admits he is of small account, and God challenges him further and describes the mighty Behemoth.
more: God asks whether a faultfinder will contend with the Almighty.
Job lays his hand on his mouth and says he will speak no more.
God asks whether Job would condemn him to be justified, and invites him to humble the proud.

41.line: God describes Leviathan, a fearsome creature no human can capture or tame.
more: He asks whether Job can draw it out with a fishhook.
Its scales, breath, and strength make weapons useless against it.
It is king over all the sons of pride.

42.line: Job repents before God, the friends are rebuked, and God restores Job with double his former possessions.
more: Job confesses he spoke of things too wonderful for him, and now his eye sees God.
God says the friends have not spoken rightly as Job has, and Job prays for them.
Job receives new children, lives 140 more years, and dies old and full of days.
